blocks.basis: The first player to bring all four pieces to the innermost square wins.
The starting squares double as marked safe squares where any number of pieces can stand.
Landing on an opponent's piece on a non-safe square sends it back to its starting square.
A throw of 4 or 8, or a hit, earns a bonus throw in the same turn.
A piece needs a precise throw to reach the finishing square, and a larger value leaves it unmoved.
Players alternate turns around the board.
If the last sown counter lands in the player's own store, the player moves again.
The player with the most counters in their store wins.
Players take turns sowing their counters.
The paper describes it as a simple solitaire mancala game, one player moving all stones into the Ruma.
The player whose turn it is may trade with the others on whatever terms they offer.
Roads, settlements and cities are built by paying resource costs, such as one lumber, one brick, one grain and one wool for a settlement.
Players begin their turn by rolling for production, then trade and build.
A greenhouse gas tracker raises risk as settlement grows, and crisis cards flip number tokens so hexes produce less.
The scenario is built to start dialogue about global warming.
Players win by developing and distributing a vaccine before the disease infects all of humanity, and lose together if they fail.
The competition is all players against the game, who win or lose together.
The game is built to teach the vaccine development process.
It simulates five stages of vaccine development, from pathogen identification to distribution.
Five phases are linked by transitions, where the result of one phase sets up the next.
Players score a point for each organism they categorise correctly.
Players take turns guessing the category of a card in the reef layout.
Players can reason from which categories are already revealed and taken to what a card is likely to be.
The design needed strong educational value, teaching people to recognise reef organisms.
Students run a paper simulation of viral spread, then deploy an intervention that changes the probability of spread and run it again.
The game is a print and play teaching tool where students gather and graph data.
Lit spaces, Sanctuary spaces, shortcuts and bus stops each have their own rule.
The players win together if all of them reach home before the timer runs out.
Players win collectively, and players already home can still pass cards to others.
Dice decide whether a player walks, but Guardian cards can counter Threat cards.
The game is made to reflect inequalities of walking alone in public spaces.
Players take turns rolling the dice.
Imbalance is built into the rules to produce an intentionally unfair experience that reflects real inequalities.
Each round has a negotiation phase between the two protagonists.
A game master manages the sequence of play and updates the players on events.
Players take the parts of Russia and Ukraine in the crisis.
A 30 minute debriefing follows the three rounds.
Actions such as buying or moving assets have costs, and expensive ones need a debate with the adjudicators.
Any piece is captured by sandwiching it between two enemy pieces.
Capturing was defined as flanking an enemy piece from the side or rear.
Pieces reaching the opposite side are promoted.
The paper links it to the custodian capture rule, where a piece is taken when trapped between two enemies along a line.
